To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) The Rumelhart and Mc Clelland model of past-tense inflection is empirically inadequate.

(a) modern NLP architectures, in particular Encoder Decoder models, can be applied to the task of learning the English past tense, (b) these architectures can learn to perform this task without any simplifying assumptions about the data, and (c) these architectures can achieve high accuracy on the past tense task.

* The Encoder-Decoder network architecture, a type of recurrent neural network that is widely used in natural language processing today, can be used to model the English past tense system in a way that avoids many of the criticisms that Pinker and Prince raised against Rumelhart and McCelland's 1986 model.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
modern neural networks are capable of modeling the past tense problem, and that the debate between Pinker and Prince and Rumelhart and Mcclelland is not as clear cut as previously thought.

we have shown that modern recurrent neural networks are able to learn the past tense mapping in a similar manner to human learners, and that they do so without any need for the kind of ad hoc mechanisms that Pinker and Prince proposed.

the past tense mapping is a much simpler problem than Pinker and Prince suggested.
